analogy: Handling PII is like a school nurse keeping medical notes. She writes down only what she needs, keeps the notes in a locked drawer, blacks out names before sharing a report with the head teacher, and shreds old notes at the end of the year. Where it breaks: a paper note is in one place, but data in an LLM app gets copied into logs, caches, vector stores and maybe a model provider's servers, so 'shred it' means finding every copy.

scale.title: Redacting 300,000 call-centre transcripts a day before they reach an LLM
scale.html:
Assumptions: an Indian insurer transcribes 300,000 calls a day, about 1,200 words each, and sends them to an LLM for summaries and quality scoring. Each call mentions on average 3 person names, plus phone numbers, policy numbers and sometimes card numbers.

  1. Structured PII first. Regex for emails, phone numbers, policy IDs and cards. For cards, add a Luhn checksum test so a 16-digit policy number is not mislabelled as a card.
  2. Names and addresses need a model. Use a named-entity detector such as Microsoft Presidio (docs). Name mentions per day: 300,000 x 3 = 900,000.
  3. Plan for misses. If your measured name recall is 95%, then 900,000 x 0.05 = 45,000 names a day still get through. Redaction lowers risk; it does not remove it. So the downstream stores still need access control and retention limits.
  4. Pseudonymise, do not just delete. Replace each name with a consistent token per call ([PERSON_1], [PERSON_2]) so the summary still reads sensibly. Keep the token-to-name map in a separate, tightly controlled store for 30 days in case an agent must follow up.
  5. Redaction points. Before the transcript is logged, before it is sent to the model provider, and on the model's output before it is stored, because the model can still echo values that slipped through.
  6. Measure it like a model. Hand-label 500 transcripts, report recall and precision per entity type each release, and track the missed-entity count per day as a risk number leadership understands.
  7. Deletion requests. Under GDPR Article 17 (text) and similar laws, a customer may ask for erasure. Because every store is keyed by call ID, you can delete the transcript, its vectors, cached summaries and trace spans in one job.

lab.look_for: The lab's input and output guardrails include a simple redaction step before text is logged to the JSONL traces. Send a request containing an email address and a card-like number and check what lands in the trace file. Then try a name: a regex-based guard will usually miss it, which is exactly the gap this lesson describes.

quiz.q: Your regex redactor catches 99% of emails and cards. A privacy reviewer still flags the logs. What is the most likely gap?

options.t: Unstructured PII such as names, addresses and free-text health details, which regex cannot reliably detect.
options.why: Correct. Structured identifiers have patterns; names and addresses do not. You need a model-based detector and still assume some misses.

options.t: The regex is too slow.
options.why: Speed is not a privacy issue. The issue is what it cannot see.

options.t: Emails should be hashed instead of masked.
options.why: Hashing can be useful for joins, but it does not address the categories regex misses entirely.

options.t: Logs should be stored as JSON.
options.why: The format does not change whether PII is in them.

quiz.q: A customer asks you to delete their data. It was used to fine-tune a model last quarter. What is true?

options.t: Removing it from the weights generally means retraining or re-fine-tuning without that data; deleting the source rows alone does not remove what the model learned.
options.why: Correct. That is why personal data should be kept out of training sets in the first place, with clear lineage of what went in.

options.t: Deleting the training file is enough.
options.why: The model's weights were already updated from it. The file is only one copy.

options.t: Asking the model to forget the person works.
options.why: A prompt cannot change weights. At best it hides outputs, unreliably.

options.t: Fine-tuned models never memorise individual records.
options.why: Models can memorise and reproduce rare strings from training data. You cannot assume they do not.

exercises.q: List every place a single customer chat might be copied in a typical RAG support app.
exercises.a: The chat database, application logs, trace spans (prompt and answer), the LLM provider's request logs (check their retention terms), any semantic or exact-match cache, analytics events, the eval or golden set if someone copied it there, support tickets created from the chat, backups of all of the above, and the vector store if conversations are indexed. Each is a place where redaction, access control and deletion must apply.

exercises.q: Your team wants to send customer emails to a hosted LLM API. List the questions you must answer before turning it on.
exercises.a: What data categories are in the emails (identifiers, financial, health)? Does the provider train on API data by default, and how long does it retain requests? In which region is data processed, and does that meet your legal requirements? Can you redact before sending without breaking the task? Do you have a data processing agreement? Can you delete or exclude a specific customer's data later? Is there a self-hosted or in-region option for the most sensitive subset? Write the answers down with links to the provider's terms, and review when the terms change.

exercises.q: Design a PII handling pipeline for an LLM-based analytics feature on a warehouse table with 50 million customer rows.
exercises.a: 1) Classify columns once with a scanner plus human review: direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers (pin code, birth date), free text. 2) Never send direct identifiers to the model; replace them with stable surrogate keys in a view. 3) For free-text columns, run batch redaction (regex plus NER) into a redacted copy, and log per-entity counts. 4) Grant the LLM job access only to the redacted view through a service account. 5) For aggregates, enforce minimum group sizes (for example, no group under 20 customers) to limit re-identification. 6) Outputs go through the same redactor before storage. 7) Deletion: a job keyed on customer ID removes rows from source, redacted copy, caches and indexes. 8) Measure redaction recall quarterly on a labelled sample.

interview.q: Where can PII leak in an LLM application?
interview.a: In logs and traces, which often store full prompts and answers. In calls to third-party model APIs, where data leaves your infrastructure. In model outputs, where the model may repeat sensitive input or reveal data retrieved for another user. In caches and vector stores that hold copies of conversations or documents. And in training or fine-tuning data, where it can be memorised. OWASP lists this as LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure. The basic defences are data minimisation, redaction at each boundary, access control, retention limits and the ability to delete.

interview.q: How would you evaluate a PII redaction system?
interview.a: Build a labelled set of realistic texts, with every PII span marked by type, including hard cases such as Indian names, addresses written in mixed scripts and numbers that look like cards but are not. Measure recall and precision per entity type, because missing a card number is worse than over-masking a city. Report misses as an expected count at production volume, for example 45,000 names a day, so the residual risk is clear. Re-run on each change to patterns or the NER model, and sample production output to check for drift.

interview.q: A multi-tenant SaaS RAG product must guarantee one customer's data never appears in another's answers. How do you design for that?
interview.a: Enforce isolation in retrieval, not in the prompt. Every chunk carries a tenant ID, and every vector query includes a mandatory tenant filter applied by the server from the authenticated session, never from model output. Consider separate indexes or namespaces for large tenants. Caches are keyed by tenant. Traces and evals are partitioned by tenant with access control. Test it: automated cross-tenant probes in CI that query tenant A with tenant B's secrets and expect nothing. Monitor for any retrieved chunk whose tenant does not match the session, and treat one occurrence as an incident. Then add output scanning as a second layer.

analogy: Content moderation is like having two lifeguards at a pool, one checking who comes through the gate and one watching the water. Even a well-trained swimmer can get into trouble, so the water lifeguard is there no matter what. Where it breaks: lifeguards rarely stop someone who is fine, but a moderation model often blocks harmless messages, so you have to count how many good swimmers you turned away, not just how many rescues you made.

scale.title: Setting a moderation threshold for a kids' learning app with 500,000 messages a day
scale.html:
Assumptions: 500,000 messages a day, of which about 1% (5,000) are actually unsafe. You built an eval set of 2,000 labelled messages, half unsafe and half edgy-but-fine, and measured the classifier at two thresholds. The rates below are example measurements, not published figures.

  1. Threshold A (strict). Catches 92% of unsafe messages, wrongly blocks 6% of safe ones.
    Missed unsafe: 5,000 x 0.08 = 400 a day. Wrongly blocked: 495,000 x 0.06 = 29,700 a day.
  2. Threshold B (looser). Catches 85%, wrongly blocks 1%.
    Missed unsafe: 5,000 x 0.15 = 750 a day. Wrongly blocked: 495,000 x 0.01 = 4,950 a day.
  3. Read the trade. B lets 350 more unsafe messages through per day but stops wrongly blocking about 24,750 children asking normal questions. Neither is free.
  4. Split by category. For a kids' app you might use the strict threshold for sexual content and self-harm, where a miss is serious, and the looser one for mild insults, where false blocks hurt learning most.
  5. Route, do not only block. Self-harm signals go to a supportive scripted reply with help resources, not a cold refusal.
  6. Cost and latency. Running a local classifier such as Llama Guard 3 (available on Ollama) on input and output adds two classification calls per message. Measure the added p95 latency and run the input check in parallel with retrieval to hide most of it.
  7. Re-measure monthly. Sample 500 production messages, label them, and recompute both rates, because slang and topics drift.

lab.look_for: The lab wraps the model with input and output guardrails and logs each decision. Send one clearly unsafe request and one edgy-but-fine one (for example a biology homework question about how viruses spread) and check both decisions. If the second is blocked, you are looking at a false positive, which is the cost side of this lesson's threshold trade-off.

quiz.q: Your moderation filter blocks 8% of legitimate questions in a health-information app. What is the right first move?

options.t: Measure false positives by category on a labelled set of real questions, then adjust the policy or threshold for the categories causing them.
options.why: Correct. Over-blocking is a measurable error just like missed harm. Tune with data per category.

options.t: Turn moderation off for health questions.
options.why: That removes the backstop entirely, including for genuinely harmful requests in that domain.

options.t: Accept it; safety always comes first.
options.why: Blocking 8% of real users is a product failure and pushes people to less careful sources. Both error types matter.

options.t: Ask the main model whether each blocked message was really unsafe.
options.why: That brings back the shared-blind-spot problem and does not tell you which category is miscalibrated.

exercises.q: A moderator flags 1,200 messages a day; humans review them and find 300 truly unsafe. Separately, a sample shows it misses about 100 unsafe messages a day. Compute precision and recall.
exercises.a: Precision = true positives / flagged = 300 / 1,200 = 0.25. Recall = true positives / all unsafe = 300 / (300 + 100) = 0.75. The filter catches three quarters of the harm but 75% of what it flags is fine, so 900 legitimate messages are blocked or queued each day. Whether that is acceptable depends on what happens to flagged messages: a soft review queue tolerates low precision better than a hard block does.

exercises.q: Streaming responses show tokens as they are generated, but your output moderator needs full text. How do you moderate a streamed answer?
exercises.a: Options: 1) buffer and check in chunks, for example every sentence or 200 tokens, so the user sees text with a short delay and you can stop the stream and replace what was shown if a chunk fails; 2) run a fast lightweight check on each chunk and the full classifier on the complete answer, retracting if the final check fails; 3) for high-risk categories or audiences, do not stream at all. Log every retraction because it shows where the model needed the backstop.

exercises.q: Design the moderation policy and evaluation for an internal tool used by a trust-and-safety team who must read abusive content to do their job.
exercises.a: Moderation here protects the business without blocking the work. Policy: the tool may summarise and classify abusive content and quote it; it must not generate new abusive content, and it must not help find real people's private details. Use a custom policy in the safety classifier that distinguishes quoting or analysing from creating. Access is limited to the T&S team with audit logs. Eval: 300 real analysis tasks that must succeed (quoting slurs inside a classification is allowed) and 200 generation requests that must be refused. Track task success and leak rate separately, and review with the T&S lead monthly, because they know what blocks their work.

interview.q: Why moderate both input and output?
interview.a: Input moderation blocks clearly disallowed requests before you spend a model call on them and lets you respond appropriately. Output moderation is the backstop: even with a safe input, or after a jailbreak, the model can still produce harmful text, and the output check catches it before the user sees it. They catch different failures, so using both gives defence in depth. Both should use an independent classifier, not the main model judging itself.

interview.q: How do you choose moderation thresholds?
interview.a: Build a labelled eval set from your own domain with both unsafe messages and legitimate edgy ones. Measure recall on unsafe content and false-positive rate on legitimate content, per category, at several thresholds. Convert the rates into daily counts at your traffic so the trade-off is concrete. Then pick thresholds per category based on the cost of each error for your users: strict for self-harm or sexual content in a kids' app, looser for mild language. Re-measure regularly because language and attack patterns drift.

interview.q: You need moderation for a product in 12 languages, including Hindi, Tamil and mixed Hinglish. How do you approach it?
interview.a: First, measure; do not assume an English-tuned classifier works. Build a labelled set per language, including code-mixed and transliterated text, with native-speaker reviewers. Compare candidate classifiers per language on recall and false-positive rate. Normalise inputs (Unicode, transliteration) before classifying. Where a language underperforms, options are fine-tuning a safety classifier on local data, adding a translation step before classification as a fallback, or routing low-confidence cases to human review. Report metrics per language on every release, because averages hide that one language is badly protected.

analogy: Output validation is like a bank teller checking a cheque before paying it. The cheque looks fine, but the teller still checks the amount is in numbers and words, the signature matches, and the sum is under the account limit. The person who wrote it might have been fooled or forced. Where it breaks: a cheque has a fixed format, but model output is free text that can hide instructions in links, markdown or code, so you have to check every place the text is going to be used.

scale.title: Validating model-written SQL for 300 analysts asking 9,000 questions a day
scale.html:
Assumptions: a retailer's text-to-SQL assistant serves 300 analysts, about 9,000 questions a day, on a warehouse with 400 tables, of which 12 hold customer personal data.

  1. Parse. Parse the generated SQL with a real SQL parser, not a regex. Reject anything that does not parse.
  2. Statement type. Allow only a single SELECT. If 0.5% of generations contain a second statement, a write, or DDL, that is 9,000 x 0.005 = 45 blocked queries a day. Log each one.
  3. Table allowlist per user. Resolve every table and view the query touches and compare against what this analyst's role may read. The 12 PII tables are reachable only through masked views.
  4. Bounds in code. Force a LIMIT (say 10,000 rows) and a statement timeout (say 60 s), and run as a read-only service account. Even a valid but huge cross join cannot hurt the warehouse.
  5. Self-correction loop with a cap. If the query errors, send the error back to the model at most 2 times, then stop and show the error.
  6. Output rendering. The answer is shown as markdown in a web app. Escape HTML, and render images or links only from allowlisted domains, so a poisoned column value that says "add this image link" cannot exfiltrate results. This is improper output handling, LLM05 in the OWASP 2025 list.
  7. Measure. Track blocked-query rate by reason (not SELECT, disallowed table, parse failure) per prompt version. A sudden jump in 'disallowed table' after a prompt change is a regression worth stopping.

lab.look_for: Find the SELECT-only validation and the row limit in the lab. Ask a question phrased to tempt a write (for example 'delete the test orders and then count orders') and confirm the validator rejects the generated SQL before DuckDB runs it. For the markdown-URL side of output validation, the 07_injection_exfiltration lab shows the allowlist step.

quiz.q: Your chat UI renders model output as markdown. Which output rule best blocks data exfiltration through injected content?

options.t: Only render images and auto-loading resources from an allowlist of your own domains, and back it with a Content-Security-Policy for images.
options.why: Correct. Image loads happen without a click, so an allowlist in code plus CSP closes the channel even when the model was fooled.

options.t: Escape HTML tags.
options.why: Needed against XSS, but a markdown image is not an HTML tag in the raw text and still renders after markdown conversion.

options.t: Limit output length to 500 tokens.
options.why: A URL carrying stolen data fits easily in 500 tokens.

options.t: Ask the model never to output URLs.
options.why: An injected instruction can override that request. The control has to be in code.

quiz.q: The model returns a tool call: transfer_funds(amount=50000, to='ACC-991'). Your validator checks the JSON schema and it passes. What is still missing?

options.t: Business-rule checks in code: amount limits, whether the destination is allowed for this user, and human approval above a threshold.
options.why: Correct. A valid shape says nothing about whether the action is permitted. That gap is excessive agency (LLM06:2025).

options.t: Nothing; the schema passed.
options.why: Schema validation checks structure only. A well-formed request can still be harmful.

options.t: A longer system prompt about safe transfers.
options.why: Prompt wording can be overridden; limits must be enforced outside the model.

options.t: Retrying the call to see if the model gives the same answer.
options.why: Consistency does not mean permission. A hijacked model can repeat the same bad call.

exercises.q: Name the right sanitiser for each sink: (a) model text inserted into a web page, (b) model-chosen values in a SQL WHERE clause, (c) model-chosen shell command.
exercises.a: (a) HTML-escape it or set it as text content, never innerHTML, plus a Content-Security-Policy. (b) Parameterised queries with the values validated against type and allowed ranges; never string-format SQL from model output. (c) Avoid it: map the model's choice to a fixed allowlist of commands with validated arguments, run in a sandbox with no network and least privilege. Free-form shell from a model is the riskiest sink.

exercises.q: A model writes product descriptions that are published to your website by a nightly job. Supplier spec sheets feed the prompt. List the output checks the job needs.
exercises.a: Escape or sanitise HTML with a strict allowlist of tags (p, ul, li, strong). Strip or allowlist links and images so supplier-planted URLs cannot appear. Check claims against the spec sheet for regulated fields (price, warranty, certifications), since a wrong warranty claim is a legal risk. Scan for PII or internal notes leaking from the spec sheet. Enforce a length range. Run a content moderation check. Anything failing goes to a review queue instead of being published, and the job reports counts per failure reason.

exercises.q: Design an output validation layer for an agent with 15 tools, so adding a 16th tool is safe by default.
exercises.a: Each tool is registered with a typed argument schema, a risk level (read, write, outbound, irreversible), and a policy function. The executor, not the model, runs: schema validation, then the policy (for example recipient must be the requesting user; amount at most 100 without approval; paths inside the workspace), then a check on data flow, so values derived from untrusted content cannot be used as outbound destinations, then approval for high-risk levels. A tool with no policy defaults to 'needs approval'. Every decision is logged with the reason. CI includes red-team cases per risk level. The safe default means a forgotten policy fails closed, not open.

interview.q: Why is model output untrusted?
interview.a: Because it is shaped by everything in the context, including text an attacker controls through injection, and because models make mistakes. If you put output straight into a web page you risk XSS; into SQL, injection; into a tool call, unintended actions; rendered as markdown, data leaking through image URLs. OWASP calls this Improper Output Handling, LLM05 in the 2025 list. So you validate and sanitise output for its destination, exactly as you would any user input.

interview.q: How do you validate a model's tool calls before executing them?
interview.a: Parse the call into a typed schema and reject anything malformed. Check the tool name against an allowlist for this user and session. Validate arguments against business rules in code: ranges, allowed recipients, paths, ownership of the resource. Check where argument values came from; values copied from untrusted documents should not become destinations for outbound actions. Require human approval for irreversible or high-value actions. Log every call and decision. The model proposes; the code decides.

interview.q: How would you stop a coding agent from being tricked by a malicious README into leaking secrets?
interview.a: Assume the README will succeed in steering the model. Do not let secrets be reachable: run the agent in a sandbox without production credentials, with environment variables scrubbed. Restrict network egress to an allowlist (package registry, the company's git host), so there is nowhere to send data. Validate commands against an allowlist, and require approval for network, credential or file-outside-repo operations. Scan outputs and diffs for secret patterns before they leave the sandbox. Log every command. This turns a successful injection into a blocked request in a log.

analogy: Defence in depth is like the layers protecting a castle: a moat, then a wall, then a gate with guards, then a locked room for the treasure. An attacker who swims the moat still faces the wall. Where it breaks: castle layers fail for different reasons, but if all your LLM layers are themselves LLMs reading the same text, one clever trick can fool several at once, so the layers must be different kinds of things, not copies of each other.

scale.title: How much do stacked defences really cut 10,000 attack attempts a month?
scale.html:
Assumptions: a public support agent with a refund tool sees 10,000 injection or misuse attempts a month. The pass-through rates are example measurements from your own red-team runs.

  1. Input moderation lets 60% of attempts through (injections often look like normal text): 10,000 x 0.6 = 6,000.
  2. Prompt hardening and spotlighting stop most; 30% still steer the model: 6,000 x 0.3 = 1,800.
  3. Least-privilege tools. The agent can only refund the logged-in customer's own orders. Only 5% of the steered attempts ask for something inside that scope: 1,800 x 0.05 = 90.
  4. Hard limits and human approval. Refunds over a set amount need a human; reviewers reject 95% of suspicious ones: 90 x 0.05 = 4.5, so about 4 or 5 bad refunds a month, each capped at the approval threshold.
  5. The independence trap. Multiplying rates assumes the layers fail independently. If moderation and prompt hardening are both LLMs and the same phrasing fools both, the real number is higher. Measure end-to-end on the full pipeline, not only per layer.
  6. Make the last layer deterministic. The tool scope and amount cap are plain code. They do not get fooled by wording, which is why they carry most of the weight. Research designs such as CaMeL push this further by tracking data flow in code (arXiv 2503.18813).
  7. Monitoring closes it. Every blocked or approved-then-reversed refund is logged, reviewed weekly, and added to the red-team suite, so next month's numbers are measured against this month's attacks.

lab.look_for: The lab measures attack success rate three times, adding a layer each run: no defence, spotlighting or delimiting, then output URL allowlist plus tool permission check. Read it as a defence-in-depth table: the prompt-level layer reduces the rate, and the code-level layer is what drives it to zero. Turn off only the spotlighting and keep the allowlist to see which layer is carrying the load.

quiz.q: Your pipeline uses an LLM for input screening, an LLM for prompt hardening checks and an LLM for output review. Red-team tests show one phrasing beats all three. What is the design flaw?

options.t: The layers are not independent; they share the same weakness, so they fail together. Add deterministic code-level controls such as tool scopes, allowlists and limits.
options.why: Correct. Stacking only works when layers fail for different reasons. Code does not get persuaded by phrasing.

options.t: You need a fourth LLM layer.
options.why: Another layer with the same weakness adds cost but little protection.

options.t: The models are too small.
options.why: Larger models are also persuadable. The problem is correlated failure, not size.

options.t: Defence in depth does not work for LLM apps.
options.why: It works when the layers are genuinely different in kind.

exercises.q: Put these controls in request order and mark which are deterministic code: output URL allowlist, input moderation classifier, tool permission check, spotlighting of retrieved text, human approval, trace logging.
exercises.a: Order: input moderation classifier (model), spotlighting of retrieved text (prompt technique), tool permission check (code), human approval (human), output URL allowlist (code), trace logging (code, runs throughout). The deterministic ones are the tool permission check, the URL allowlist and logging; human approval is independent of the model. Those are the layers an injection cannot talk its way past.

exercises.q: Red-team results: 2,000 attempts; 1,100 pass input moderation; 280 of those steer the model; 14 of those reach a tool call inside the allowed scope; 1 gets human approval. What is the pass rate of each layer and the end-to-end success rate?
exercises.a: Moderation pass rate 1,100 / 2,000 = 55%. Steering rate 280 / 1,100 = 25.5%. In-scope tool rate 14 / 280 = 5%. Approval rate 1 / 14 = 7%. End to end 1 / 2,000 = 0.05%. Note that you measured end to end directly, which already includes any correlation between layers; that is more trustworthy than multiplying layer rates from separate tests.

exercises.q: You have budget for one engineer-month to harden an existing agent. How do you decide where to spend it?
exercises.a: 1) Run the red-team suite end to end and record, for each successful attack, which layers it passed. 2) Rank by impact: a leak of customer data or money movement outranks rude text. 3) Look for the cheapest deterministic control that blocks the top paths: usually narrowing tool scopes, adding recipient or amount limits, or an output URL allowlist, each a few days of work. 4) Next, add monitoring for the attack patterns you saw, so new variants are noticed. 5) Only then tune prompts or classifiers. Re-run the suite after each change and report end-to-end success rate before and after, so the month's work has a measured result.

interview.q: What does defence in depth mean for an LLM app?
interview.a: It means using several independent safeguards so one failure does not become a breach. A typical stack is input moderation, prompt hardening that marks untrusted text as data, least-privilege tools, hard limits and human approval for risky actions, output validation and moderation, and monitoring. Each layer is imperfect; together they make an attack need several things to go right. The most important layers are deterministic code controls like tool scopes and allowlists, because they cannot be talked around.

interview.q: Why is least privilege considered the strongest layer against prompt injection?
interview.a: Because it limits the damage regardless of whether the model is fooled. Prompt defences and classifiers reduce how often an attack works, but none reach zero. If the agent can only read the current user's records and only send email to that user, a fully successful injection has little to steal and nowhere to send it. It is also deterministic code, so its strength does not depend on wording. In OWASP terms, it directly addresses LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency.

interview.q: How would you report the security posture of an LLM agent to a risk committee?
interview.a: I would give a short threat model listing assets, entry points and the top risks with scores. Then measured numbers from the red-team suite: end-to-end attack success rate per risk category, current versus last quarter, with sample sizes. Then the controls per risk, marked as deterministic or probabilistic, and the worst-case impact if all probabilistic layers fail, for example 'maximum refund without approval is capped by code'. Production indicators: blocked attempts, approvals, incidents. And open gaps with owners and dates. Mapping each risk to the OWASP 2025 IDs helps the committee compare with other systems.
